title: The Integrated Life: Refusing the Sacred and Secular Divide
subtitle: Somewhere you learned that faith belongs to a part of your life and the rest belongs to you. Sunday is God's. Monday is yours. This is the capstone lie of a divided age, and it is a lie. There is one life, under one Lord, and not a single square inch of it is exempt. What it means to refuse the sacred and secular divide, and to live whole.

parts.title: The Two Drawers
parts.body:
You keep your life in two drawers and you did not decide to. One drawer holds the things you think of as spiritual. Prayer, church, the Bible you mean to read more, the offering, the moments you feel close to God. The other drawer holds everything else. The commute. The spreadsheet. The argument with your spouse about the dishwasher. The promotion you want and the coworker you cannot stand. The vast majority of your waking hours live in the second drawer, and somewhere along the way you came to believe that God lives mostly in the first.

So you pray before the meal and then conduct the meal as though the praying were over. You worship on Sunday and clock in on Monday as a different person with a different set of rules. You would never lie in a prayer meeting and you shade the truth in a sales call without a flicker of unease, because the sales call is in the other drawer, the one God does not check. You are not a hypocrite in the way the word is usually thrown. You are something quieter and more common. You are divided. You have a faith and a life, and they touch at the edges and rarely in the middle.

Here is what no one told you. The dividing was the whole problem. You did not inherit a faith that politely confines itself to a religious corner of an otherwise secular existence. That arrangement would have been unthinkable to Abraham, to David, to Paul, to Jesus, to anyone who took the living God seriously before roughly the last three hundred years. The idea that there is a neutral, secular zone where God has no particular claim, a public square swept clean of him, a Monday that belongs to you, is not ancient and it is not Christian. It is a modern invention, and you have been formed by it more deeply than you know.

Notice how naturally the divide runs in you. You call the pastor's work ministry and your own work merely a job, as though God cared about the one and tolerated the other. You feel holy in the sanctuary and ordinary in the office, holy when you pray and ordinary when you parent, as if the diaper and the prayer belonged to different kingdoms. You would be embarrassed to bring your faith into a budget meeting and you do not notice that the embarrassment is itself a confession, a confession that you have agreed to keep God in his drawer where he will not make trouble at work.

We built this divide and then wondered why our faith felt thin. We made God a hobby and called the rest of life real, and then complained that he seemed distant on Tuesday. He was not distant. We had assigned him a room and told him to stay in it. The thinness was not his absence. It was our architecture, and the architecture is a cage we built ourselves and then mistook for the shape of the world.

parts.title: What the Divided Life Costs
parts.body:
A divided life does not merely offend a doctrine. It slowly dismantles a person, and the cost is paid in coin you do not notice leaving your pocket. The first cost is integrity in its oldest sense, the state of being integrated, of one piece, undivided. A person with a faith in one drawer and a life in the other is by definition not integrated, and the word for that is not balance. The word is fracture. You become a set of selves who do not fully know one another, the Sunday self and the Monday self, the prayer self and the deal self, and the seams between them are exactly where the rot gets in.

The second cost is to your witness, and the watching skeptic finds the seam before you do. He is not impressed by your doctrine and he is not waiting for your argument. He is waiting to see whether the God you confess on Sunday governs the way you handle a refund, a rumor, a subordinate, a hard week. When he sees that your faith stops at the church door, he does not conclude that you are a bad Christian. He concludes that Christianity is the kind of thing that stops at church doors, a private comfort with no public consequences, a hobby that makes no claim on the real world. Your divided life is not a private matter. It is an argument, and it is an argument against the gospel, delivered more persuasively by your Monday than your Sunday could ever undo.

The third cost is to the world itself, the parts of it you have quietly written off as secular and therefore beyond redemption. If your work is just a job and not a calling, you will do it for the paycheck and never ask what it is for, never ask whether it builds or corrodes the human good, never bring the mind of Christ to a single decision that shapes how other people live. If your politics, your art, your science, your money, your parenting are secular zones where faith does not reach, then you have handed the largest territories of human life over to be governed by other gods, and you have done it in the name of keeping your faith pure. The divide does not protect the faith. It surrenders the world.

And there is a fourth cost, the most intimate. The divided life is exhausting in a way you may have stopped noticing because you have never lived any other way. Performing wholeness while living in fragments takes enormous energy, the energy of keeping the drawers from spilling into each other, of remembering which self goes in which room, of managing the dissonance between the man who prays and the man who schemes. People come to my study worn down to the grain and cannot name why, and often the answer is this. They are tired because they are two. The integrated life is not first a duty. It is a rest, the rest of finally being one person before one God, with nothing left to hide in the second drawer because there is no second drawer.

parts.title: One Lord Over Every Square Inch
parts.body:
Scripture has no sacred and secular divide because Scripture begins with creation. In the beginning God made the heavens and the earth, all of it, the sea and the dry land and the creeping things and the working week, and after each day he called it good, and after the whole he called it very good. There is no neutral matter in the Bible, no zone of the world that came from somewhere other than God and therefore belongs to someone other than God. The dirt is his. The body is his. The economy of Eden, the tending and keeping of the garden, the naming of the animals, the making of culture, all of it is given as worship before a single religious rite is mentioned. Work comes before the fall. Cultivation is not a concession to a broken world. It is the original commission of an unbroken one.

So when the Bible speaks of worship it refuses to keep it in a building. Whatever you do, Paul writes to the Colossians, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. And to the Corinthians, whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. Eating. Drinking. Whatever you do. The apostle cannot find the secular drawer because for him it does not exist. He tells slaves to work as for the Lord and not for men, which means the most ordinary and even degraded labor is reframed as service rendered directly to Christ. He tells the Romans to present their bodies, not their souls only, their bodies, as a living sacrifice, and calls this their reasonable worship. The body, the work, the meal, the daily grind, the whole of it is the altar. Nothing is left over to be merely secular.

The Old Testament had already shattered the divide with one devastating image. On the day of the Lord, Zechariah prophesies, even the bells of the horses shall be inscribed Holy to the Lord, and every cooking pot in Jerusalem shall be as sacred as the bowls before the altar. The horse bells. The kitchen pots. The most ordinary objects of common life made as holy as the temple vessels. This is not the temple expanding its hours. It is the temple bursting its walls, the holiness that lived in one room flooding out to claim the whole city, the whole of life. The trajectory of the entire Bible runs toward a day when the distinction between sacred and secular space collapses entirely, and John sees it consummated in Revelation, a city with no temple in it, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, and the whole city is the holy place.

Jesus himself lived the integration he came to restore. He spent the overwhelming majority of his earthly life not preaching but working, swinging a hammer or a saw in a Galilean workshop, and the Father called those silent ordinary decades beloved before a single sermon was preached. When he taught, he taught from the secular world the religious teachers had stopped seeing, the farmer scattering seed, the woman losing a coin, the manager juggling debts, the laborers grumbling about their wages, the wedding running out of wine. He did not draw his lessons from the temple. He drew them from Monday, because Monday was never godless. He took bread and wine, the most common food on the most common table, and made them the center of Christian worship forever, so that the faith could never again pretend that the holy and the ordinary live in separate rooms.

The deepest ground of the integrated life is the lordship of Christ, which Scripture insists is total or it is nothing. He is, Paul writes to the Colossians, the one in whom all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, and in him all things hold together, and he is before all things. All things. He is given a name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. There is no constituency exempt from that lordship, no square foot of the creation over which the risen Christ does not say, mine. To confess Jesus as Lord and then to fence off your work, your money, your politics, and your private hours as a secular zone where his lordship does not reach is not a smaller faith. It is a different religion wearing Christian clothes, a religion in which Christ is Lord of the sanctuary and you are still lord of your life. The gospel will not let you keep that arrangement. It comes for the whole.

parts.title: Kuyper, the Reformers, and the Long War on the Divide
parts.body:
The phrase that has organized this conviction for the modern church belongs to Abraham Kuyper, the Dutch theologian, journalist, and prime minister who in 1880 stood to open the Free University of Amsterdam and said the sentence that will not stop ringing. There is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry, Mine. Kuyper was not inventing a novelty. He was naming an ancient conviction with new force for a world that had just finished building the sacred and secular divide into its universities, its governments, and its imaginations. He spent a public life refusing to hand any sphere of human activity over to a godless autonomy, founding a newspaper, a university, and a political party on the conviction that Christ claims art and science and commerce and statecraft as surely as he claims the church, and that the believer who retreats from those spheres has not kept the faith pure but has abandoned the field.

The roots run deeper than Kuyper, back to the Reformation, which struck the divide its hardest historical blow. The medieval church had drawn a sharp line between the religious life, the calling of monks and priests and nuns who were thought to do the truly holy work, and the secular life of the merchant, the farmer, and the mother, who were thought to do the ordinary work and to be holy only at one remove. Martin Luther tore that line apart. He taught that the dairy maid milking her cow and the magistrate governing his city and the parent changing a child are doing work as fully pleasing to God as any monk at his prayers, that vocation, calling, belongs to the shoemaker as much as to the priest, and that God milks the cow through the milkmaid. The shoemaker, Luther said, does his Christian duty not by putting little crosses on the shoes but by making a good shoe, because a good shoe serves the neighbor and serving the neighbor is the love of God made visible. The entire economy of ordinary work was reconsecrated in a sentence.

John Calvin built this into a whole vision of life lived before the face of God, coram Deo, every act of it, the public and the private, the religious and the common, performed in the presence of a God who is everywhere and exempts nothing. The Puritans who inherited Calvin carried this conviction across an ocean and into the founding of a new world. They saw the building of a town, the running of a farm, the keeping of accounts, and the raising of children as spiritual labor, sanctified callings, not interruptions of the religious life but the religious life itself worked out in soil and ledger and household. They were so serious about the integration of faith and work that they sometimes overcorrected into a grim and joyless industry, and we should learn from their excess as well as their insight, but they never made the modern mistake of thinking that God cared only about the chapel and not about the field.

Then came the long secularization that the philosopher Charles Taylor has mapped with such care in his account of how the West moved from a world in which belief was the air everyone breathed to one in which it became one option among many, and a contested one. Over several centuries, beginning in earnest in the seventeenth and eighteenth, the West invented something genuinely new, a public sphere imagined as neutral, godless by default, a secular space from which religion was politely asked to withdraw into the private heart. The sociologist Peter Berger called this the sacred canopy coming down, the shared roof of meaning under which a whole society had lived being dismantled until faith became a personal preference rather than a public reality. The tragedy is that the church, instead of resisting this arrangement, largely accepted it, agreeing to keep faith in the private drawer the modern world had assigned it, trading the lordship of Christ over all of life for a protected little corner where religion could feel safe. Lesslie Newbigin, returning to England after decades as a missionary in India, saw it with the clear eyes of an outsider and named it. The West had become the most secularized culture on earth precisely because it had accepted a public square swept clean of God, and the church had largely surrendered without a fight. Newbigin spent his last years calling the church to take back the field, to refuse the privatization of the faith, and to bring the gospel as public truth into the very spheres the modern divide had declared off limits. That call is the inheritance this domain is built to carry forward.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The conviction that Christ claims every square inch makes the believer free to learn from anyone who has thought hard about how a whole life hangs together, while testing each account against the One who actually holds all things together. The thinkers below have each seen something real about integration, fragmentation, or the secular age, and each must be measured against Scripture, because every account of the unified life carries a hidden picture of what the life is unified around.

secular.author: Charles Taylor
secular.whatItGetsRight: Taylor gives the most patient account we have of how the West came to imagine a godless public world as the default. He shows that secularism is not the simple subtraction of faith from a neutral world but a positive construction, a new way of experiencing the self as buffered and self-contained rather than open to a world charged with God. He helps the believer see that the sacred and secular divide is not the obvious truth it pretends to be but a particular and recent achievement that could have been otherwise.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Taylor describes the cage with unmatched precision and stops at its door. He is a careful Catholic, but his account is largely diagnostic, mapping how we came to feel the world as disenchanted without finally proclaiming the One who actually fills it. Scripture does not merely explain the buffered self. It pierces it, insisting that in God we live and move and have our being, that he is not far from any one of us, that the heavens declare his glory whether the modern self feels it or not. The believer needs Taylor's map to understand the country, and then needs the Word to be set free from it, because understanding the cage does not open the door. Only the risen Christ who claims every square inch does that.

secular.source: Drive and the science of meaningful work
secular.author: Daniel Pink
secular.whatItGetsRight: Pink and the research on motivation demonstrate that human beings are not finally moved by carrots and sticks but by autonomy, mastery, and purpose, that work performed merely for the wage corrodes the worker, and that people flourish when their labor is connected to something larger than themselves. This is a real and useful confirmation that the merely secular account of work as a transaction for money is too thin to sustain a human life, and that we are built to need our work to mean something.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Pink locates the larger something in the worker, in personal purpose and self-chosen mastery, and Scripture relocates it outside the self entirely. The purpose that finally heals work is not a meaning you generate but a Lord you serve, working as for the Lord and not for men. Pink can tell you that meaningless work is corrosive and cannot tell you what work is finally for, because the answer is not found in human psychology but in the commission to cultivate and serve a world that belongs to God. A purpose manufactured by the self is one more thing the self must sustain by its own effort, and it leaves the deepest fragmentation untouched, because the self that needs to be unified cannot be the thing that unifies it.

secular.source: The sociology of the privatized self
secular.author: Robert Bellah and the Habits of the Heart team
secular.whatItGetsRight: Bellah and his colleagues documented with care how modern Americans came to speak of their deepest commitments in the language of private preference, how even religious conviction became a matter of personal taste held in a sphere walled off from public life, a faith one shops for and customizes rather than a truth that governs. They named the way the modern self has been trained to keep its values in a private drawer and to regard the public world as a neutral marketplace, and they saw that this leaves people lonely and societies thin.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Bellah names the privatization brilliantly and offers no Lord to end it, only a hope for renewed communities of memory. Scripture refuses the private drawer at the root, because the faith it proclaims is not a preference held in the heart but a public fact about who owns the world. Jesus is Lord is not a value the believer prefers. It is a claim about reality that does not become false when the public square ignores it. Bellah can show you that the privatized faith is corroding the common life, and only the gospel can supply the conviction that dissolves the private drawer, the conviction that there is no neutral marketplace because Christ already cried Mine over the whole of it.

secular.author: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
secular.whatItGetsRight: Csikszentmihalyi studied the states in which people are most whole, most absorbed, most undivided, and found that human beings flourish when consciousness is ordered rather than scattered, when attention is unified toward a worthy challenge rather than fractured across competing demands. His work confirms from the side of psychology that the divided and distracted self is a diminished self, and that integration, the ordering of the whole person toward a single end, is not a luxury but a condition of a life that feels worth living.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Csikszentmihalyi finds that the ordered self flourishes and cannot say what to order the self around, treating the worthy goal as interchangeable, a chess game or a symphony or a surgery, so long as it absorbs. Scripture insists that the integration is only as good as its center, and that a life unified around the wrong treasure is not healed but only efficiently lost. Augustine saw what flow theory cannot, that the soul is restless until it rests in God, that the only ordering that finally heals the fractured self is the love of God that gathers all our scattered loves into one. The psychology describes the unified state with great care and leaves untouched the question of what is worth being unified by, which is the only question that matters.

secular.source: Bowling Alone and the collapse of shared life
secular.author: Robert Putnam
secular.whatItGetsRight: Putnam documented the long decline of the institutions in which Americans once lived a common and integrated life, the clubs, congregations, unions, and neighborly bonds that wove private persons into a public fabric. He showed with data that the retreat of the self into a private and curated existence has measurable costs in trust, health, and happiness, and that a society of disconnected individuals, each tending a private drawer, is a society slowly coming apart at the seams it can no longer see.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Putnam diagnoses the fragmentation of the common life and prescribes more association, more joining, more social capital, which is true as far as it goes and cannot reach the depth of the wound. Scripture knows that the bonds between persons fray because the bond between the person and God has frayed first, that horizontal isolation follows vertical estrangement. The church is not finally one more voluntary association to be revived for its civic benefits. It is the body of Christ, a communion grounded in a reconciliation Putnam cannot supply, and the integration of human life with human life that he rightly longs for is finally a gift of the gospel that first integrates human life with God.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who agree entirely that Christ is Lord of all of life still differ, and have differed for centuries, over how the church should engage the spheres the modern world calls secular. The question is not whether to refuse the divide but how, whether the believer is mainly called to transform the institutions of the world or mainly called to build a faithful counter-community that bears witness against them. Hear each at its strongest, because both are trying to honor the same lordship and both are guarding against a real and opposite danger.

views.body: This view, often called the transformationist or Kuyperian vision, holds that because Christ claims every square inch, the believer is called to enter the institutions of the world and bend them toward his lordship from the inside. The Christian belongs in the university, the statehouse, the studio, the laboratory, and the marketplace, not as a quiet infiltrator but as a redemptive presence laboring to make these spheres what God meant them to be. Advocates point to Joseph in Egypt, Daniel in Babylon, and Esther in Persia, believers who took the levers of pagan power and used them for the good of many, and to the whole biblical commission to cultivate and steward the creation. They argue that the world is not a sinking ship to be abandoned but a field to be tended, that culture is not the enemy but the assignment, and that to withdraw from the spheres is to surrender them to other gods by default. The danger they are guarding against is real, a retreating faith that builds its own walls, lets the world go to ruin, and calls its abdication holiness, leaving art and science and government to be shaped entirely by people who do not know the Lord. Against that retreat they hold that the salt is meant to be rubbed into the meat, that the light is meant for the whole house, and that a faith too pure to get its hands dirty in the secular spheres has misunderstood the very lordship it claims to confess. They warn, soberly, that the danger of their own position is co-option, that the believer who enters the halls of power to transform them can be transformed by them instead, and they insist the answer is not retreat but vigilance, a presence in the world that keeps its allegiance clear.

This view, often associated with the witness of the church as a contrast society, holds that the first and most powerful way the church refuses the divide is by being a genuinely whole community, a people whose common life under Christ is itself the argument the world cannot make. Advocates point out that the early church changed the Roman world not by capturing its institutions, which it could not, but by being an integrated community so visibly different in how it handled money, sex, power, the poor, and death that the watching empire could not explain it away. They argue that when the church rushes to transform the world from within before it has been formed into a distinct people, it is the church that gets absorbed, baptizing the agendas of the age and losing the very gospel it came to bring. The faithful counter-community comes first, a people thick enough in its own life to resist the spirit of the times, and only such a people has anything worth carrying into the wider spheres. The danger they are guarding against is also real, a triumphalist faith that grabs for cultural power, fuses the gospel with a political or economic program, and ends up indistinguishable from the world it set out to change, a salt that has lost its savor. Against that, they hold that the church must be the church before it tries to fix the world, that the integrated life is first learned and embodied in a community of disciples, and that the most subversive thing believers can do in a fragmented age is to live whole together where the world can see it. They acknowledge, in turn, the danger of their own position, a withdrawal that becomes self-protective and abandons the neighbor, and they insist the counter-community exists not for itself but for the life of the world it is sent to serve.

parts.title: What Integration Forms in a Person
parts.body:
The integrated life is not first a belief you hold but a person you slowly become, and the becoming is the work of years, not the result of a decision. You cannot will yourself whole in an afternoon. You are made whole the way a fractured bone is made whole, slowly, under pressure, by a power working in you that you did not supply, and along the way God forms specific things in the one who stops living in two drawers.

He forms a single self where there used to be several. The first and strangest gift of integration is that you stop being so many people. The Sunday self and the Monday self begin to merge, the prayer self and the work self stop being strangers, the public man and the private man are gradually reconciled until there is just one person, the same in the sanctuary and the office and the kitchen and the dark. This is what the Bible means by integrity, and it is not mainly about honesty in the narrow sense. It is about being of one piece, undivided, the same all the way through, so that what you confess and what you do and who you are have stopped contradicting one another. People who have been long in the company of an integrated person often cannot say what is impressive about them, only that there is a restfulness there, the restfulness of someone who has nothing in a second drawer to hide.

He forms the eyes to see the holiness of the ordinary. The divided person looks at the commute and the spreadsheet and the laundry and sees dead time, secular time, the unspiritual stretches between the holy moments. The person being integrated slowly loses that blindness. He begins to see the diaper change as worship, the honest invoice as an act of love, the well-made thing as a service to the neighbor and therefore to God, the ordinary Tuesday as ground every bit as holy as the Sunday it used to envy. The horse bells become holy. The cooking pots become sacred. Nothing is merely secular anymore, and the whole of life takes on a weight and a meaning it never had when most of it was filed under ordinary.

He forms courage in the spheres the believer used to keep quiet. Integration makes a person harder to intimidate into the private drawer. The man who has come to believe that Christ is Lord of his work cannot easily go back to leaving his faith at the office door, not because he becomes obnoxious about it but because his whole way of working has been claimed, and the claiming shows. He brings the mind of Christ to a budget, a hiring decision, a quarrel, a temptation to cut a corner, and he does it not as a performance but as the natural overflow of a life that has stopped pretending God only cares about church. This courage is quiet, mostly, lived in the integrity of a thousand small decisions, but it is real, and the watching world can feel it.

And he forms rest, the deepest formation of all. The exhaustion of the divided life, the constant labor of keeping the selves apart and the drawers from spilling, finally lifts. There is a peace that comes from being one person before one God with nothing left to hide and nothing left to compartmentalize, and it is not the peace of having an easy life but the peace of having an undivided one. Augustine named the whole of it in a single sentence at the opening of his Confessions. You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. The restless heart is the divided heart, scattered across a hundred loves and a dozen selves and two drawers. The rest is integration, the gathering of the whole fractured self into one, around the only center large enough to hold it, the Christ in whom all things, including the pieces of you, hold together at last.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Integration is not achieved by resolving to be whole. It is built the way a wall is built, one stone at a time, by carrying the lordship of Christ into one previously secular corner of your life and then another, until there are no corners left where he is a stranger. None of what follows will make you whole by next month. All of it will start to close the seam between your faith and your life if you keep at it. Begin with the one drawer you most resist opening to him, and work from there.

steps: Name your two drawers out loud. Take ten minutes and write down honestly which parts of your life you treat as spiritual and which parts you treat as merely secular, the zones where God feels relevant and the zones where he feels absent. The map is the first step, and most people have never drawn it.

Pick the most ordinary task on your calendar this week, the dullest secular thing on it, and do it consciously as worship. Whatever you do, do it as for the Lord. Notice what changes when the spreadsheet or the errand is offered to God instead of merely endured.

Catch yourself once using the language of the divide. The word just, as in just a job, just the kids, just the dishes. Each just is a confession that you have filed something under secular. Replace it once and watch what the replacement does to the task.

Pray once at the start of a workday for the work itself, not for strength to get through it but for the work to be good, useful, honest, a service to whoever it touches. Let the prayer claim the eight hours the divide had written off.

Read Colossians slowly, the whole letter, watching Paul refuse the divide. In him all things hold together. Whatever you do, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus. Let the letter retrain your sense of where the lordship of Christ reaches, which is everywhere.

Take the one sphere you most want to keep secular, the one place you least want God to have an opinion, and ask honestly why. The thing you most want to fence off is usually the thing his lordship most needs to enter. Bring it into a single specific prayer.

Find another believer and confess the divide to each other. Where do you live as though God does not check. Naming it to one trusted person breaks its quiet power, because the divide thrives in the dark and dies a little in the telling.

Reconsider one decision you would normally make on purely secular grounds, a purchase, a hire, a calendar choice, and ask what the lordship of Christ has to say about it. Not a verse. A direction. Let his claim touch a decision it used to skip.

Audit your week by the hour and ask of each block, does Christ govern this. The commute. The work. The screen. The meals. The conversations. The audit will show you the exact shape of your divide, the zones still living in the second drawer, and you cannot integrate what you have not seen.

Reclaim your work as vocation, not job. Spend a season asking what your particular labor is for, whom it serves, what good it builds in the world, and how the love of neighbor takes shape in doing it well. Luther said God milks the cow through the milkmaid. Find the cow you are milking.

Bring your money fully under his lordship, since money is where the divide hides most stubbornly. Build a giving and a budgeting practice that treats every dollar as belonging to God, and watch the drawer marked finances stop being secular.

Pick one sphere you have surrendered to other gods by default, the news you consume, the entertainment you absorb, the way you handle conflict, and deliberately bring the mind of Christ to bear on it for a whole season. Take back one square inch of the field.

Aim, over years, at a single self, the same person in the sanctuary and the office and the dark. Make integrity in its oldest sense your long ambition, not flawlessness but wholeness, a life with nothing left in the second drawer because you have ceased to keep one.

Let the lordship of Christ keep expanding into territory you once thought neutral. Each year, find one more sphere of your life that you had quietly fenced off as secular and open the gate. The work of integration is never finished this side of the new creation, and that is not discouragement but direction.

Build a household and a circle that lives whole, where faith is not confined to a religious corner but governs how you work, spend, rest, argue, and treat the stranger. The integrated life is best learned in company, and the most subversive witness in a fragmented age is a people who live undivided where the world can see it.

Keep returning to the center that holds the pieces. The integration is only ever as deep as its rest in Christ, in whom all things hold together, including the scattered fragments of you. Read Augustine once a year, until being one person before one God has stopped being a discipline and become simply who you are, your heart at rest at last in the One it was made for.
